extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners interested in philosophical method and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: A prescriptive methodological guide for how to conduct one's reason and seek truth in the sciences, including epistemic rules and provisional moral maxims to govern inquiry and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never accept anything as true without clear and distinct perception
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first was never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such; that is to say, carefully to avoid precipitancy and prejudice, and to comprise nothing more in my judgement than what was presented to my mind so clearly and distinctly as to exclude all ground of doubt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid precipitancy and prejudice. Limit judgment to what appears clearly and distinctly to the mind so as to exclude all reasonable doubt. Treat unclear or doubtful opinions as provisional until they meet this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide difficulties into as many parts as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: “The second, to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break complex problems into simpler, manageable components to address each adequately. Use analytic partitioning to make reasoning tractable and to avoid conflating distinct issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order thoughts from simplest to most complex (stepwise ascent)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The third, to conduct my thoughts in such order that, by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step, to the knowledge of the more complex; assigning in thought a certain order even to those objects which in their own nature do not stand in a relation of antecedence and sequence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start inquiry with the simplest, most evident truths and proceed incrementally to more complex conclusions. When necessary, impose an order on subjects to allow stepwise deduction and accumulation of certitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make complete enumerations and general reviews to avoid omission
rubrics_metrics.description: “And the last, in every case to make enumerations so complete, and reviews so general, that I might be assured that nothing was omitted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure thoroughness by enumerating all conditions and performing broad reviews so as to detect and eliminate omissions. Use exhaustive checks to secure completeness of argument or solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical/general representations (geometry and algebra) for relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes recommends considering relations or proportions in the most general form, representing them by straight lines for clarity, and expressing aggregates by brief characters so as to borrow the advantages of geometrical analysis and algebra while avoiding their defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, translate problems into general relations (proportions), use geometric representation (e.g., straight lines) to render simple objects distinctly imaginable, and employ symbolic notation to handle aggregates. This permits clear deduction and reuse of simple truths in discovering further results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor a few simple, reliably observed precepts over a multitude of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes criticizes the many precepts of formal logic and similar arts as often injurious or superfluous and asserts that four simple precepts suffice, provided one steadfastly observes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a small set of clear methodological rules rigorously applied, rather than adhering to a large, cumbersome body of procedural prescriptions that may confuse or mislead inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisory Moral Maxim 1: Obey laws and adopt the moderate opinions of those around you
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first was to obey the laws and customs of my country, adhering firmly to the faith in which, by the grace of God, I had been educated ... and regulating my conduct in every other matter according to the most moderate opinions, and the farthest removed from extremes, which should happen to be adopted in practice with general consent of the most judicious of those among whom I might be living.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While suspending final judgment in inquiry, conform your practical conduct to the laws, customs, and moderate opinions of the judicious persons among those with whom you live. Prefer moderation in practice and avoid binding commitments that limit future revision of beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisory Moral Maxim 2: Be firm and resolute in action; act on the most probable
rubrics_metrics.description: “The second maxim was to be as firm and resolute in my actions as I was able, and not to adhere less steadfastly to the most doubtful opinions, when once adopted, than if they had been highly certain ... when it is not in our power to determine what is true, we ought to act according to what is most probable ... and afterwards consider it, in so far as it relates to practice, as no longer dubious, but manifestly true and certain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical decisions, choose one course (preferably the most probable) and commit to it in action to avoid paralysis and remorse. Treat the chosen practical hypothesis as certain for conduct, even if it remains epistemically uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisory Moral Maxim 3: Conquer yourself rather than fortune (adjust desires)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The third maxim was to endeavor always to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world, and in general, accustom myself to the persuasion that, except our own thoughts, there is nothing absolutely in our power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on changing one’s own desires and internal responses instead of attempting to alter external circumstances beyond control. Cultivate the recognition that only one’s thoughts are wholly within one’s power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit reforms to one's own opinions rather than public institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes counsels against attempting large-scale public reforms unless one is called or enabled to do so; his aim is the reformation of his own opinions, not the overturning of states or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply methodological reform personally—use the method to rework your own beliefs—rather than attempting wholesale changes to public orders, which are complex and may be harmful if disrupted precipitously.
